“And so,” I concluded, laying down the morning’s paper, “it appears our good Inspector Davies has yet another perplexing case upon his hands. A retired professor, vanished without a trace from his study, leaving behind naught but a half-finished chess game and an unlit pipe.”

Professor Thorne, who had been meticulously cleaning a particularly ancient brass microscope, barely glanced up. “A pity, Alistair, but hardly a challenge worthy of our combined intellects. The domestic imbroglio and the desperate flight of the embarrassed academic are tales as old as time itself, and their solutions rarely demand more than a diligent constabulary and a week’s perseverance.”

“But the absence of any note, Thorne, or struggle,” I countered, “and the house locked from within, save for a pantry window slightly ajar but leading to a sheer drop of some twenty feet. It smacks of something far more intricate.”

“Indeed,” he replied, with a faint smile, “and yet the Inspector’s telegram, which arrived a scant hour ago, makes no mention of these intriguing particulars. His sole request was that I cast an eye over an ‘object of curiosity’ found lodged in the ornamental shrubs below said window. He promises to retrieve it this evening, but knowing my impatience, and his own, he saw fit to dispatch it to my rooms by a young constable of remarkable agility.” He gestured with a linen cloth towards a dark, slender object resting upon a velvet cushion on a nearby table. “Behold, then, the solitary clue, Dr. Finch, the silent witness to Professor Armitage’s peculiar disappearance.”

I rose and approached the table, my curiosity piqued despite Thorne’s dismissive tone. It was a walking stick, of a dark, polished wood, likely rosewood or ebony. The handle, intricately carved in the form of a griffin’s head, showed signs of considerable wear, particularly on the left side. The shaft was slender, and the brass ferrule at the tip was deeply scored.

“A rather handsome piece,” I observed, turning it over in my hands. “Antique, I should imagine, and of some value. The carving is quite exquisite.”

“A fine observation, Alistair, but one that leads us little further than the obvious. Tell me, what else can you glean from this unassuming article?” He leaned back in his armchair, his keen eyes fixed upon my expression.

I examined it more closely. “The wood is dark, as I said, but there are faint, almost imperceptible scuffs along the lower shaft, as if it has been dragged along rough stone. The handle, too, seems to have been gripped with considerable force for extended periods, judging by the smooth, almost burnished quality of the wood.” I ran my finger over the worn areas. “And there is a peculiar, almost sweet, earthy odour emanating from the tip, distinct from the polish.”

“Excellent, Alistair, you see, but you do not deduce. You catalogue, you describe, but the implications remain veiled to your otherwise acute perceptions. Pray tell me, for instance, from what humble particulars do you discern that the owner of this stick is a man of intellectual pursuits, recently plagued by acute anxiety, and possessed of a peculiar nocturnal habit which has, in the last three days, entirely altered?”

I blinked, momentarily speechless. “My dear Thorne, you jest! You conjure an entire biography from a mere stick of wood! How on earth can you draw such precise conclusions?”

He chuckled softly, a rare sound. “Not jest, Alistair, but the logical application of observable fact. Permit me to demonstrate. First, the man is a scholar, perhaps a professor, as the Inspector’s telegram suggested. Observe the peculiar flattening of the carving on the left side of the griffin’s head, precisely where the thumb would rest. This is not the wear of mere walking, but of hours spent leaning, supporting the weight of the head, doubtless over books or papers. The slight indentation where the index finger curls speaks to a habitual grip, not one of casual support.”

“But his anxiety?” I pressed, intrigued.

“Ah, that is a subtle inference, yet entirely clear. Note the minute, almost microscopic splintering along the very edge of the ferrule, and the faint, almost imperceptible discoloration, a fine, greyish powder, caught in the deeper scoring. This is not the dust of the street, nor the grime of a common thoroughfare. This, my dear Finch, is the residue of fine slate dust, a substance peculiar to the roofs of houses, and often found lodged in the older, less maintained chimneys.”

“But how does that indicate anxiety, Thorne, and this nocturnal habit?” I asked, utterly bewildered.

“Consider, Alistair. A scholar, as we have established, a man of routine and order. This stick, though old, has been meticulously maintained, save for this recent damage. The slate dust suggests a recent and repeated contact with the roof. Why would a man, particularly one advanced in years and presumably of fixed habits, suddenly take to scaling his own roof, not once, but several times, and always at night?” He picked up a small vial from his desk. “This, by the way, is the remnant of the dust scraped from the window ledge. An identical match.”

“He might be checking his chimney,” I suggested, though even to my own ears it sounded rather weak.

“A possibility, certainly, but then why the anxiety? The fervent, almost desperate way in which the stick has been pressed into service for this new pursuit suggests a profound disturbance. Furthermore, observe the nature of the damage. The stick has not merely been rested against the roof; it has been used as a lever, repeatedly, perhaps to prise something open, or to test a weak point, or even to prevent a fall. This requires considerable exertion, and would be undertaken only if the stakes were exceptionally high, suggesting a mind troubled by some grave concern, and seeking a means of ingress or egress beyond the conventional.”

“And the alteration of his habit?”

“The stick, as you correctly noted, Alistair, is of good quality and has been well-cared for. Yet, the deep scoring on the ferrule, quite recent, betrays its use on rough stone, entirely inconsistent with the polished floors and paved paths a scholar of his standing would normally traverse. This recent, sudden shift from a sedentary life to one involving rooftop excursions is the alteration. The very act of taking to the roofs, of using a walking stick as a tool for leverage and balance in the dark, points to a man utterly consumed by a secret, a man who believes he cannot use the door.”

He paused, allowing his words to sink in. “And the anxiety, you see, is directly linked to this desperate, surreptitious activity. What could drive a respected academic to such undignified lengths, repeatedly climbing onto his roof at night, leaving trails of slate dust, and employing his walking stick as a crude implement, if not a profound and consuming anxiety, or perhaps, a terrifying premonition?”

Just then, a sharp rap echoed from the street door, and I heard the heavy tread of Inspector Davies upon the stairs. Thorne merely smiled, a flicker of satisfaction in his eyes. “Our solutions, Alistair, often appear to be plucked from the ether, but they are, in truth, merely the logical consequences of the facts observed.” He turned the walking stick over gently, his gaze lingering on the worn griffin’s head. “I trust the Inspector’s news will illuminate the precise nature of Professor Armitage’s anxiety, and the purpose of his peculiar, nocturnal forays upon the rooftops of his old house.”

Inspector Davies, a man whose usual demeanour was one of stolid professional competence, now stood in the doorway with an expression that combined perplexity with an almost discomfiting awe. His broad frame filled the aperture, and his eyes, usually fixed upon the practicalities of the immediate case, seemed to hold a distant, troubled light. He removed his bowler hat with a gesture that was less habitual and more a nervous distraction, revealing a forehead creased with something beyond mere exertion.

“Thorne, Alistair,” he began, his voice a little gruffer than usual, “I trust I do not intrude upon your breakfast, but matters at Professor Armitage’s residence have taken a turn, and a most perplexing one at that.”

Thorne, who had been meticulously polishing a delicate chemical balance with a square of chamois leather, merely gestured with the implement towards the two armchairs facing the fireplace. “Not at all, Inspector. We are precisely at the point of expecting you. Alistair and I have been discussing the curious case of Professor Armitage’s walking stick, and we find ourselves rather eager to hear the developments which I am certain you bring.”

Davies settled into an armchair, his gaze falling upon the walking stick which Thorne had placed carefully upon a small, polished side table. He eyed it with a mixture of recognition and a fresh layer of confusion, as if seeing it anew through Thorne’s inexplicable pronouncements.

“Well,” Davies continued, running a hand over his close-cropped hair, “the long and short of it, Thorne, is that Professor Armitage has vanished.”

Alistair, who had been pouring a second cup of coffee, nearly dropped the pot. “Vanished, Inspector? But how? When?”

“Precisely the questions, Alistair, that are currently causing us no end of bother,” Davies replied, shaking his head. “Our men were dispatched this morning, as you requested, Thorne, to keep a discreet watch, given the Professor’s recent, shall we say, uncharacteristic behaviour. They reported in at six, noting that the house remained dark, the curtains drawn, and no sign of life within. At eight, when there was still no movement, and given the Professor’s strict habits, they grew concerned. They knocked, rang, and receiving no answer, finally obtained a warrant to enter.”

“And what did they find?” Thorne inquired, setting aside his chamois leather and fixing the Inspector with his keen, unwavering gaze.

“A house in perfect order, Thorne, meticulously kept, precisely as one would expect from a man of the Professor’s scholarly disposition,” Davies explained. “No signs of a struggle, no forced entry, no theft that we can immediately ascertain. Every book was in its place, every paper neatly stacked upon his enormous oak desk. The fire in the hearth was cold, suggesting he had retired at his usual hour. His bed was slept in, but no Professor. It was, for all intents and purposes, as if the man had simply dematerialised into the ether. Save for one detail, a rather significant detail, which my men found most peculiar.”

Davies reached into the inner pocket of his coat and produced a small, flattened velvet pouch, which he laid upon the table with an almost reverent care. He untied the drawstring, and from within he extracted a single, curious object. It was a coin, Alistair observed, but unlike any he had ever seen. Larger than a sovereign, yet thinner, made of a dark, almost black metal, and bearing upon its surface an intricate, if somewhat corroded, relief of some ancient, horned deity. It possessed an undeniable antiquity, and a certain unsettling power, even to the casual glance.

“This, Thorne,” Davies announced, his voice hushed, “was found beneath the Professor’s pillow. It is made, we believe, of electrum, or some alloy known only to the ancients. A note was tucked beneath it, bearing a single word, scribbled in the Professor’s hand: ‘Fell.’ Our forensics chap, a fellow with a good eye for these things, says the script is unusually shaky, almost as if written in haste or under duress. And there, Thorne, is where the trail ends.”

Thorne picked up the coin, turning it over between his long, slender fingers. He examined the horned deity, tracing the intricate patterns with a detached, clinical interest, yet his eyes gleamed with an almost preternatural understanding. He then carefully placed the coin back into its pouch, and pushed it gently across the table towards Davies.

“The plot thickens, Inspector, most satisfactorily,” Thorne observed, a faint smile playing upon his lips. “Professor Armitage, a man of precise habit, meticulous in his arrangement of books and papers, yet so disturbed as to leave his bedchamber and then vanish, leaving behind a single, enigmatic coin and a cryptic note stating ‘Fell.’ And no sign of him since?”

“None whatsoever, Thorne. Not a trace, not a single witness, not a whisper. It is as if the very night consumed him,” Davies confirmed, a hint of frustration entering his voice. “We have searched the house from cellar to attic, questioned the neighbours, though they claim to have seen nothing out of the ordinary. His study, his library, everything is as it should be. It is a puzzle of the most exasperating kind.”

“And yet, Inspector, it is a puzzle whose pieces we have already begun to assemble,” Thorne remarked, turning his gaze towards the walking stick. “Alistair, you will recall my deductions regarding the Professor’s profound anxiety, his nocturnal rooftop forays, and the precise manner in which this stick had been pressed into service.”

Alistair, though still grappling with the sheer audacity of Armitage’s disappearance, nodded slowly. “Indeed, Thorne. The slate dust, the scored ferrule, the recent damage to the shaft. You inferred a man consumed by some grave concern, resorting to climbing his own roof at night.”

“Precisely,” Thorne affirmed, his eyes now alight with a characteristic brilliance. “Now, Inspector, you state that the Professor vanished, leaving behind a single, ancient coin and a note saying ‘Fell.’ I put it to you, that the professor did indeed ‘fall,’ but not in the conventional sense of succumbing to an illness, nor merely failing in some endeavour. He fell from his roof.”

Davies stared, his mouth agape. “From his roof, Thorne? But why? And where is the body? There are no signs on the ground, no broken tiles, no disturbance to the garden below!”

“Ah, Inspector, the absence of evidence is not the evidence of absence, especially when the circumstances are as peculiar as these,” Thorne countered, leaning forward slightly. “Consider the facts. My initial observations, derived purely from this most eloquent of walking sticks, pointed to a scholar of routine and order who had, quite recently, developed a profound and desperate need to ascend to his rooftop, and not once, but repeatedly, at night. The stick itself shows signs of being used as a lever, or perhaps as a brace, to prevent a fall, or to assist in a precarious ascent or descent.”

Thorne then rose and picked up the walking stick, holding it up for emphasis. “The deep scoring on the ferrule, Inspector, is not merely from rough stone. It is consistent with repeated, strenuous contact with slate tiles, particularly when employed for purchase on a sloping surface. The recent damage to the shaft, the splintered wood near the grip, this suggests a sudden, violent strain, far beyond the ordinary demands of a scholar’s nocturnal promenade. This is the damage of a man struggling, perhaps losing his footing, or grappling with a difficult task in the dark.”

“And the anxiety,” Alistair interjected, now beginning to see the convergence of the lines of thought. “You said his anxiety was profound.”

“Indeed, Alistair. What could drive a respected academic, a creature of habit, to such undignified and perilous nocturnal exertions, repeatedly scaling his own roof, if not a consuming anxiety related to something of immense value, or perhaps a secret he sought to protect or recover?” Thorne explained, his voice gaining momentum. “Now, the coin, Inspector. This ancient electrum, with its horned deity. Is it of any particular significance, to your knowledge, in Professor Armitage’s vast field of classical studies?”

Davies’s expression shifted from bewilderment to a sudden flicker of understanding. “By Jove, Thorne, it is! Professor Armitage was a leading authority on the Mithraic mysteries, the ancient Roman cult. This symbol, the horned deity, it’s a representation of Mithras himself, often depicted with a Phrygian cap and sacrificing a bull. The coin itself, if genuine, is incredibly rare, possibly unique. He has been searching for such an artifact for decades, or so I recall from his various academic publications. He believed such a coin, a ‘Mithraic Obulus’ as he termed it, could unlock secrets to the cult’s origins that have long eluded scholars.”

“There we have it, Inspector. The motive, the object of his anxiety,” Thorne declared triumphantly. “Professor Armitage was not merely climbing onto his roof; he was attempting to recover or secure this Mithraic Obulus. The repeated nocturnal forays suggest the object was either exceptionally well-hidden, or the means of accessing it was fraught with difficulty, perhaps even danger. The stick, with its lever marks, implies he was attempting to pry open a concealed compartment, a secret niche, perhaps within the very structure of his roof.”

“But the note, ‘Fell’?” Alistair pressed. “How does that connect to a fall from the roof if there’s no body?”

“A most astute question, Alistair, and one that leads us to the heart of the matter,” Thorne replied, a glint in his eye. “Let us not be so literal in our interpretation of ‘fell.’ Consider a scholar’s world. What does one possess that can ‘fall’ and yet remain hidden, inaccessible, perhaps even irrevocably lost, beyond the reach of human hands? A book. A manuscript. A delicate scroll.”

He paced the room, his hands clasped behind his back, his brow furrowed in thought. “The Professor’s meticulous habits, the order of his house, his lifelong pursuit of this Mithraic Obulus. He had finally found it, or perhaps, it had recently come into his possession, and he was attempting to secure it, to hide it, perhaps from unscrupulous rivals, or even from the public eye until he could properly document its significance.”

“But where would he hide such a thing on a roof?” Davies interjected, rubbing his chin.

“Ah, Inspector, the genius of concealment often lies in plain sight, or in a place so inconvenient that none but the most desperate or determined would seek it,” Thorne expounded. “Consider the architecture of these older houses. They often possess hidden nooks, forgotten dormers, or even unused chimney flues. A scholar such as Armitage, steeped in history, would be precisely the sort to know of such architectural peculiarities and to exploit them. He would know, too, that a rooftop offers both isolation and a certain, perverse security.”

“The note ‘Fell’,” Thorne continued, stopping before the window and gazing out upon the grimy rooftops of London. “It is not, I believe, a confession of his own physical fall, but a lament, a cry of despair over the loss of something profoundly precious. He had the coin, the Mithraic Obulus, perhaps in a protective casing, or within a small, valuable leather purse. He was on the roof, attempting to secure it, perhaps within a hidden compartment he was trying to pry open with his walking stick. In the dark, amidst the hazards of the rooftop, something went awry. The coin, or the package containing it, slipped from his grasp. It ‘fell.’”

Alistair gasped. “It fell down a chimney, perhaps? Or between the tiles, into some inaccessible cavity of the house itself?”

“Precisely, Alistair. The dust from the slate, the frantic use of the stick, the desperate anxiety. He had finally retrieved his life’s ambition, only to have it slip from his grasp, falling into an irretrievable void within his own house,” Thorne explained, his voice resonating with the tragedy of the hypothesis. “The note ‘Fell’ becomes a testament to this catastrophic loss, not of his person, but of the object of his lifelong quest. And the electrum coin left beneath his pillow? A desperate, final clue. The last remaining fragment of his discovery, placed there perhaps in a moment of utter despair, or as a message to those who would follow, to indicate what had been lost.”

Davies leaned back in his chair, his usual skepticism slowly giving way to a grudging acceptance. “So, you believe he was on the roof, perhaps trying to secure this coin, or a collection of similar coins, within some hidden space, and one of them, the main prize, slipped and fell into the structure of the house. And then, he vanished?”

“His vanishing, Inspector, is then a psychological consequence of this calamitous event,” Thorne theorised, resuming his pacing. “Imagine the mental state of a scholar, a man whose entire life has been dedicated to the pursuit of a singular, arcane artefact. He finds it. He possesses it. And then, through a moment of ill-fated clumsiness, or perhaps an unforeseen structural weakness in his chosen hiding place, it is lost, irretrievably, within the very walls of his home. His lifelong ambition, literally beyond his grasp, yet tantalisingly near. What does such a blow do to a man of his sensibilities?”

“It would break him, Thorne,” Alistair offered, understanding dawning fully upon him. “He would be utterly devastated. His life’s work would feel pointless, his achievement rendered meaningless.”

“Indeed, Alistair. A scholarly obsession, once shattered, can leave a man utterly bereft of purpose, of will. The anxiety I deduced from the stick, the desperate attempts to access his hidden cache on the roof, were for this very coin, this Mithraic Obulus. Its loss, after so much effort and such profound risk, would be a psychological catastrophe,” Thorne articulated, his voice now imbued with a profound sense of human understanding. “Professor Armitage, therefore, did not merely vanish; he fled. He fled from the profound disappointment, the unbearable proximity of his lost treasure. He could not bear to remain in a house that contained his lost ambition, a house that had become, for him, a tomb of his life’s work. He would have left in a state of shock, perhaps even a temporary derangement, driven by an instinct to escape the scene of his personal catastrophe.”

“So, you think he simply walked away?” Davies asked, still struggling with the sheer emotional weight Thorne attributed to a mere coin, however rare.

“Not simply, Inspector. Desperately. Without a plan, without a destination, merely driven by the crushing weight of his failure,” Thorne clarified. “He would have taken nothing but the clothes on his back, perhaps clutching this single remaining coin as a tangible reminder of his fleeting triumph and his subsequent despair. He would have descended from the roof, perhaps through the very door he normally avoided, in a trance-like state, and simply walked away into the night, seeking to put as much distance as possible between himself and the scene of his misfortune.”

“And you believe he is still alive?” Alistair inquired, his voice low.

“For the present, yes. The human spirit, even when battered, possesses a remarkable resilience,” Thorne asserted. “He is undoubtedly in a state of profound distress, perhaps wandering aimlessly, seeking some form of oblivion. But he is not, I believe, physically harmed, beyond the immediate fall and the profound emotional wound. The absence of a body, the lack of any significant disturbance to the house, all point not to foul play or a fatal accident, but to a psychologically driven flight.”

Davies stood up, slowly, his gaze moving from Thorne to the walking stick, then to the velvet pouch containing the ancient coin. “So, our task now is not to search for a body, but for a broken man. A man who has, for all intents and purposes, lost his soul within the walls of his own home.”

“Precisely, Inspector. And a man who, if found, will require the utmost sensitivity and care,” Thorne advised. “His mind, having been subjected to such an ordeal, will be fragile. The recovery of his senses, and perhaps even of the lost Mithraic Obulus itself, will be a delicate matter.”

“But how do we find him, Thorne? A man wandering aimlessly, without purpose or destination, in this sprawling metropolis?” Davies asked, a new kind of weariness settling upon his features.

Thorne returned to his small side table, retrieved his lens, and held it up, inspecting the polished glass. “We begin by understanding the nature of a scholar’s despair, Inspector. His habits, even in distress, will not entirely vanish. He will seek places of quiet, of historical resonance, places where the weight of the past might offer some solace, however fleeting. He will avoid the bustling thoroughfares, the cacophony of modern life. Libraries, museums, ancient churches, perhaps even the less frequented corners of the British Museum. These are the haunts of such a man, even in his distress. Furthermore, the coin itself might be a clue.”

“The coin?” Alistair questioned. “How so?”

“He kept one, Alistair, one single, tangible reminder of his great achievement and his great loss,” Thorne elaborated. “It is a testament to his scholarly integrity, even in his madness, that he chose to leave this particular fragment behind, a clue to the nature of his catastrophe. He might still be clutching another, perhaps the very last, a solitary solace in his wandering. And if so, it might, in a moment of lucidity, or desperation, be offered for sale, or used as a means to acquire a simple meal, or shelter. Keep an eye on the antiquity dealers, the pawnbrokers, particularly those who cater to the more esoteric tastes.”

Davies nodded, pulling out his notebook. “Very well, Thorne. A broken scholar, wandering through the ancient haunts of London, clutching a relic of his shattered dream. It is a peculiar sort of case, I must admit, but your reasoning, however unconventional, does possess a certain disturbing coherence. I shall dispatch my men with these new instructions, and with a description of the Professor and, of course, the peculiar nature of the coin.”

“One final observation, Inspector,” Thorne added, as Davies made to leave. “The Professor’s house is, I assume, now under careful guard?”

“Indeed, Thorne. My most reliable men are there. Not a soul shall enter or leave without scrutiny,” Davies affirmed.

“Excellent. Then, whilst you search for the Professor, I shall take the liberty of examining the interior structure of his roof, and the upper regions of his chimney flues, with a view to discovering the precise location where this invaluable Mithraic Obulus might have ‘fell.’ For it is often the case, Inspector, that a lost treasure, particularly one that has fallen into a confined space, is not truly lost, but merely hidden by a layer of human despair and architectural inconvenience. And a man, however broken, might still find a measure of peace in the knowledge that his life’s quest might yet be recovered, however arduous the task.”
